column9: Match each microscope part to its job.
column14: Stage clips :: Hold the slide in place
column15: Diaphragm :: Controls the amount of light on the slide
column16: Ocular lens :: Magnifies the image, usually 10x
column17: Nose piece :: Holds the objective lenses
column18: Base :: Supports the microscope from the bottom
column19: Arm :: Supports the microscope when carried and holds the body tube
column28: Stage clips hold the slide. The diaphragm controls the amount of light. The ocular lens magnifies the image, usually 10x. The nose piece holds the objective lenses. The base supports the bottom, and the arm is what you hold when carrying it.
column29: Think about what each part does while you use the microscope, from the lens at the top down to the base.

column9: Most classroom microscopes have three of these parts, in powers of 4x, 10x, and 40x. The one in use sits just above the slide. Which part is it?
column17: Objective lens
column28: The objective lenses sit just above the slide, usually in powers of 4x, 10x, and 40x. The ocular lens is the single lens at the top, the diaphragm controls light, and the body tube is not a lens at all.
column29: You switch between these to get more or less magnification.

column9: Which knob should you use when the high-power objective is in place?
column17: Neither knob; just change the light
column28: On high power, use only the fine adjustment knob; it makes tiny moves to sharpen the image. Never use the coarse knob on high power. Changing the light changes brightness, not focus.
column29: On high power you only need very small focusing changes. Which knob is made for that?

column9: What is the correct way to carry a microscope?
column14: One hand holding the body tube at the top
column15: One hand on the arm, swinging at your side
column16: Two hands: one on the arm and one under the base
column17: Two hands holding the stage on both sides
column28: Carry it upright with two hands: one on the arm and one under the base. The body tube and stage are not made to hold the microscope's weight.
column29: Which two parts are built to support the microscope?

column9: It is fine to clean microscope lenses with a paper towel or the bottom of your shirt.
column28: False. Clean lenses only with a soft cloth or lens tissue. Paper towels and clothing can scratch the glass.
column29: What could rough paper or fabric do to a glass lens?

column9: The ocular lens is 10x and the objective lens is 4x. What is the total magnification? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total magnification = ocular × objective = 10 × 4 = 40x.
column29: Total magnification: ocular lens power times objective lens power.

column9: Which objective should you always start on when you begin looking at a slide?
column17: Whichever objective is closest
column28: Always start on the lowest-power objective, then move up to the higher powers. Starting on the highest or middle objective, or on whichever one happens to be in place, breaks this rule.
column29: Think of zooming a phone camera to find something: do you start zoomed all the way in or all the way out?

column9: The eyepiece of a microscope is also called the ___ lens.
column28: The ocular lens is the eyepiece, the lens closest to your eye. Ocular comes from oculus, the Latin word for eye.
column29: This word comes from the Latin word for eye.

column9: Which part of the microscope supports the slide?
column17: Stage
column28: The stage is the flat platform that supports the slide; the stage clips hold it in place. The base supports the whole microscope, not the slide.
column29: Which flat part has a hole in the middle so light can come up through the slide?

column9: Which type of microscope gives a three-dimensional view of a whole insect or leaf?
column17: Electron microscope
column28: A stereoscopic, or dissecting, microscope gives a 3D view of whole objects like insects and leaves. A compound microscope looks at thin specimens on slides with light passing through them.
column29: Light cannot shine through a whole insect. Which microscope is built for looking at thick, whole objects?

column9: Which type of microscope is like a magnifying glass, with only one lens?
column17: Electron microscope
column28: A simple microscope has only one lens, like a magnifying glass. A compound microscope uses two or more lenses.
column29: Rule some out: the compound microscope in our classroom has an ocular and objectives, so it has more than one lens.

column9: To find total magnification, you ___ the ocular lens power by the objective lens power.
column28: Total magnification = ocular × objective. For example, 10x × 40x = 400x.
column29: 10x and 40x make 400x. What math operation does that?

column9: The coarse adjustment knob moves the stage up and down quickly for focusing.
column28: True. The coarse adjustment knob makes big, fast moves for focusing on low power. The fine adjustment knob makes small moves to sharpen the image.
column29: Coarse means rough or large. Fine means small.

column9: A microscope has a 10x ocular lens, and the 10x objective is clicked into place. What is the total magnification? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total magnification = ocular × objective = 10 × 10 = 100x. (Adding would give 20, which is a common mistake.)
column29: Multiply the two lens powers.

column9: The image under the microscope is so bright that it looks washed out. Which part should you adjust?
column17: Nose piece
column28: The diaphragm controls how much light reaches the slide. Close it a little to make the image dimmer. The knobs focus, the clips hold the slide, and the nose piece switches objectives.
column29: Which part controls the amount of light?

column9: Brayden's microscope has a 15x ocular lens. He uses the 40x objective. What is the total magnification? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total magnification = ocular × objective = 15 × 40 = 600x.
column29: Not every ocular is 10x. Multiply this ocular by the objective.

column9: A microscope has a 5x ocular lens and a 50x high-power objective. What is the total magnification on high power? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total magnification = ocular × objective = 5 × 50 = 250x.
column29: Multiply the ocular power by the high-power objective.

column9: The total magnification is 80x and the ocular lens is 20x. What is the power of the objective lens? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total = ocular × objective, so objective = total ÷ ocular = 80 ÷ 20 = 4x. Check: 20 × 4 = 80. ✓ Multiplying instead (80 × 20 = 1,600) gives a number far bigger than the total, so it cannot be the objective.
column29: Work backward: what times 20 equals 80?

column9: The high-power objective is in place. Maya turns the coarse adjustment knob two full turns to raise the stage. What is most likely to happen?
column14: The objective could crash into the slide and break it.
column15: The image would get too bright to see anything.
column16: The image would come into focus faster than with the fine knob.
column17: The specimen would flip upside down and backwards.
column28: On high power the objective sits very close to the slide. Each turn of the coarse knob moves the stage a long way, so two full turns can ram the slide into the lens and break the slide or the lens. The coarse knob moves far too much for the tiny focusing changes high power needs, it does not change brightness, and the image is upside down and backwards no matter which knob you turn.
column29: On high power, how much space is there between the lens and the slide?

column9: Mason is searching for one tiny amoeba that could be anywhere in a drop of pond water. Why is the 4x objective the best one to search with?
column14: It is the only objective with its power written on it.
column15: It shows the largest area, so the specimen is easiest to find.
column16: It makes the specimen look the largest right away.
column17: It lets in the least light, so the image is not too bright.
column28: The 4x objective has the largest field of view: it shows the most of the slide at once, which gives Mason the best chance of spotting the amoeba. The 40x objective, not the 4x, makes things look largest; every objective has its power written on it; and low power is actually the brightest setting, not the dimmest.
column29: The 4x objective makes things look smaller than the 40x does. What do you get in exchange?

column9: Why should you center the specimen before switching to high power?
column14: High power only shows the edges of the slide, so it must be in the middle.
column15: Centering makes the image brighter, so you can skip the diaphragm.
column16: The objective lens will not turn unless the slide is centered first.
column17: The field of view shrinks on high power, so an off-center specimen disappears.
column28: On high power you see a much smaller circle of the slide. If the specimen is near the edge on low power, it will be outside the view on high power.
column29: Does high power show more or less of the slide than low power?

column9: Put the steps for viewing a slide in order.
column14: Refocus using only the fine adjustment knob
column15: Watching from the side, turn the nose piece to the high-power objective
column16: Place the slide on the stage and secure it with the stage clips
column17: Carry the microscope to your desk with one hand on the arm and one under the base
column18: On the lowest-power objective, focus with the coarse adjustment knob
column19: Center the specimen and sharpen it with the fine adjustment knob
column28: Carry it safely, clip the slide on the stage, focus on low power with the coarse knob, center and sharpen with the fine knob, switch to high power while watching from the side, then refocus with the fine knob only.
column29: Start with what has to happen before you can look at anything. Then ask which steps only make sense once you can already see the specimen.

column9: Brayden switches to high power and the image looks too dim. What should he do?
column14: Turn the coarse adjustment knob a few turns
column15: Loosen the stage clips on the slide
column16: Open the diaphragm a little wider
column17: Close the diaphragm a little more
column28: Images get dimmer on high power. Opening the diaphragm lets more light reach the slide. The coarse knob should never be used on high power, the stage clips only hold the slide, and closing the diaphragm would make the image even darker.
column29: Which part controls the amount of light, and does Brayden need more light or less?

column9: A slide with the letter "e" is placed on the stage in normal reading position. How does the "e" look through the microscope?
column17: Backwards only
column28: A compound microscope flips the image both ways, so the "e" appears upside down and backwards (turned around 180°).
column29: Think of the letter e slide: which way did the opening of the e face on the stage, and which way did it face through the eyepiece?

column9: While looking through the microscope, Grace slides the slide to the LEFT. Which way does the image move?
column17: It does not move
column28: Because the image is flipped, it moves the opposite way: slide moves left, image moves right. (Slide moves away from you, image moves toward you.)
column29: The image is flipped. Does it move with the slide or the opposite way?

column9: Ella's microscope has these field-of-view widths: 4 mm at 40x, 1.6 mm at 100x, and 0.4 mm at 400x. She finds a tardigrade (water bear) about 0.5 mm long. What is the highest total magnification at which she can still see the whole tardigrade at once? (Type the number only.)
column28: To see the whole tardigrade, the field of view must be wider than 0.5 mm. At 400x the field is only 0.4 mm wide, so part of the tardigrade is cut off. At 100x the field is 1.6 mm wide, so it fits. 40x also fits, but 100x is the highest power that does.
column29: The whole tardigrade has to fit inside the circle. Compare its length with each field-of-view width.

column9: Which are proper ways to care for a microscope? Select all that apply.
column14: Wipe the ocular lens with your shirt
column15: Set it on a flat, steady surface
column16: Clean the lenses only with a soft cloth or lens tissue
column17: Use the coarse adjustment knob on high power
column18: Carry it by the body tube with one hand
column19: Carry it with one hand on the arm and one under the base
column28: Proper care: carry it with two hands (arm and base), clean lenses only with a soft cloth or lens tissue, set it on a flat surface, and don't bang it. Never use the coarse knob on high, carry it by the body tube, or wipe lenses with clothing.
column29: Good care protects the lenses and keeps the microscope from falling.

column9: Which part holds the objective lenses and the ocular lens at the proper distance apart?
column17: Base
column28: The body tube holds the ocular lens and the objective lenses the right distance apart. The arm supports the microscope when carried, the stage holds the slide, and the base supports the bottom.
column29: The ocular sits at the top end of this part, and the nose piece is attached at its bottom end.

column9: Which type of microscope uses a magnetic field instead of glass lenses to form its image?
column17: Electron microscope
column28: An electron microscope uses a magnetic field to bend beams of electrons instead of lenses to bend light, and it can magnify far more than any light microscope. Compound, stereoscopic, and simple microscopes all use light and glass lenses.
column29: Glass lenses bend light, but a magnet cannot bend light. So what must this microscope aim at the specimen?

column9: Match each type of microscope to the job it is best for.
column14: Simple microscope :: Reading tiny print in a newspaper
column15: Compound light microscope :: Viewing a thin slice of onion skin on a slide
column16: Stereoscopic (dissecting) microscope :: Getting a 3D view of a whole ant's legs and mouthparts
column17: Electron microscope :: Seeing the shape of a single virus
column28: A simple microscope has one lens, like a magnifying glass, which is enough for tiny print. A compound light microscope passes light through a thin specimen on a slide, like onion skin, and then through two or more lenses. A stereoscopic microscope gives a 3D view of whole objects, like an ant's legs and mouthparts. An electron microscope magnifies far more than any light microscope, enough to show a virus.
column29: Think about how big the object is and whether light can pass through it.

column9: Ava looks at a fresh wet mount and sees several perfectly round, completely clear circles near her specimen. What are they most likely?
column14: Cells that have been stained with dye
column15: Scratches on the ocular lens glass
column16: Air bubbles trapped under the cover slip
column17: Tiny holes in the glass slide
column28: Perfect clear circles in a wet mount are air bubbles. They form when the cover slip is dropped flat instead of lowered at an angle. Cells aren't perfect clear circles, and scratches wouldn't be round.
column29: Living cells have parts inside them and are rarely perfect circles. What else in a fresh wet mount could look round and empty?

column9: Put the steps for making a wet mount slide in order.
column14: With a pipette, add one drop of water on top of the specimen
column15: Slowly lower the cover slip onto the drop
column16: Place the specimen in the middle of a clean glass slide
column17: Place the slide on the stage under the stage clips
column18: Hold the cover slip at a 45° angle at the edge of the drop
column28: Put the specimen in the middle of the slide, add one drop of water on top of it, hold the cover slip at a 45° angle at the edge of the drop, and lower it slowly. Only then does the finished slide go on the stage under the clips.
column29: Which things have to be on the slide before you can put something on top of them?

column9: A microscope has a 10x ocular. How many times as large is the total magnification with the 40x objective as with the 10x objective? (Type the number only.)
column28: High: 10 × 40 = 400x. Low: 10 × 10 = 100x. 400 ÷ 100 = 4, so the 40x objective gives 4 times as much magnification.
column29: Find both total magnifications first, then divide the bigger one by the smaller one.

column9: Lily looks through the eyepiece on low power, but the view is completely black, not just blurry. The objective is clicked firmly into place. Which part should she check first?
column17: Coarse adjustment knob
column28: A completely black view means no light is reaching your eye at all. The light source (a lamp, or a mirror on some older microscopes) projects light up through the diaphragm, the specimen, and the lenses, so if the lamp is off, unplugged, or burned out, or the mirror is tilted away, the view goes black. The focus knobs only make the image sharper or blurrier, and the stage clips just hold the slide in place.
column29: A blurry view and a black view have different causes. For no image at all to reach your eye, what must be missing?

column9: Jace wants to switch from the 10x objective to the 40x objective. Which part should he turn?
column17: Diaphragm
column28: The nose piece holds the objective lenses and turns to click a different one into place. The body tube doesn't turn, the coarse knob focuses, and the diaphragm controls light.
column29: Which part holds all the objective lenses?

column9: On high power, Grace's microscope gives a total magnification of 800x with the 40x objective. What is the total magnification when she switches to the 10x objective? (Type the number only.)
column28: Step 1: Find the ocular. Ocular = total ÷ objective = 800 ÷ 40 = 20x. Step 2: New total = ocular × new objective = 20 × 10 = 200x.
column29: The ocular lens doesn't change when you switch objectives. Find the ocular power first.

column9: Jace put his slide on the stage, clicked in the high-power objective first, and turned the coarse knob. Now he sees only a blur. What should he do?
column14: Stay on high power and keep turning the coarse knob until the blur clears
column15: Take the slide off and look at the ocular lens closely for any smudges
column16: Close the diaphragm all the way so that less light reaches the specimen
column17: Return to low power and focus there first, then center and switch to high
column28: Jace broke two rules: start on the lowest power, and never use the coarse knob on high power. Going back to low power and focusing there fixes both. Turning the coarse knob more on high power can crash the objective into the slide, and cleaning the lens or closing the diaphragm does not fix focus.
column29: Which two microscope rules did Jace break?

column9: Through the microscope, Leah sees her specimen in the upper-left part of the field of view. Which way should she move the slide to bring it to the center?
column17: Toward the lower left
column28: The image moves opposite to the slide. To move the image down and to the right (toward the center), move the slide up and to the left. In other words, move the slide toward where the image appears.
column29: The image moves the opposite way the slide moves. Which way does the image need to go?

column9: A slide has a lowercase letter "b" in normal reading position. Which letter does it look like through the microscope?
column17: It looks like a "b"
column28: The microscope turns the image upside down AND backwards. Flipping "b" upside down gives "p"; then flipping it backwards gives "q." Flipping only backwards gives "d."
column29: Flip the letter top-to-bottom, then flip it left-to-right.

column9: At 40x, Mia counts about 50 cells lined up across the field of view. She switches to 100x. About how many cells will fit across the field of view now?
column17: 5 cells
column28: 100x is 100 ÷ 40 = 2.5 times more magnification, so each cell looks 2.5 times wider and the field of view holds 2.5 times fewer cells: 50 ÷ 2.5 = 20. Zooming in never fits more cells (125), the count does change (50), and 5 would be a 10-times jump, like going from 40x to 400x.
column29: When you zoom in, do more or fewer cells fit across? By how many times did the magnification change?

column9: On low power (100x), the field of view is 2 mm across. About how wide is the field of view on high power (400x)? Answer in mm.
column28: High power magnifies 400 ÷ 100 = 4 times more, so the field of view is 4 times smaller: 2 mm ÷ 4 = 0.5 mm.
column29: If magnification goes up 4 times, does the field of view get bigger or smaller, and by how much?

column9: On high power, the field of view is 0.4 mm across. Two paramecia lined up end to end would just stretch across the field. About how long is one paramecium, in mm?
column28: Two paramecia fill the 0.4 mm field, so one is about 0.4 ÷ 2 = 0.2 mm long (real paramecia are about 0.1 to 0.3 mm). Multiplying (0.4 × 2 = 0.8 mm) would make one paramecium longer than the whole field, which can't be right.
column29: How many paramecia fit across the field? Each one takes up that fraction of the field's width.

column9: Jordan's microscope has a 20x ocular, and he is using the 10x objective. Kaylee's microscope has a 5x ocular. She is viewing her slide at the same total magnification as Jordan. Which objective is Kaylee using?
column28: Step 1: Jordan's total = 20 × 10 = 200x. Step 2: Kaylee's objective = total ÷ ocular = 200 ÷ 5 = 40x. Check: 5 × 40 = 200. ✓ Picking 10x assumes the same objective gives the same total, but Kaylee's ocular is weaker. 25x comes from adding (20 + 10 = 30, then 30 − 5), and 1,000x fails the check: 5 × 1,000 = 5,000x, not 200x.
column29: Find Jordan's total magnification first. Then work backward using Kaylee's ocular.

column9: Ty's image is blurry and too dark on high power. Which are good fixes? Select all that apply.
column14: Take off the stage clips so the slide can move freely
column15: Open the diaphragm to let in more light
column16: Turn the coarse adjustment knob several turns
column17: Switch to an even higher-power objective
column18: Turn the fine adjustment knob slightly
column19: Adjust the light source so more light shines up through the slide
column28: Blurry on high power: turn the fine knob slightly. Too dark: open the diaphragm and adjust the light source to send more light up through the slide. The coarse knob is never used on high, the clips hold the slide steady, and a higher objective would make it even darker.
column29: One problem is focus and one is light. Which parts fix each, safely, on high power?

column9: Through the eyepiece, Owen sees a dark speck. When he moves the slide, the speck stays in the same place. When he twists the ocular lens, the speck turns with it. Where is the speck, and what should he do?
column14: On the slide, so he should make a brand-new slide
column15: On the objective lens, so he should switch to high power
column16: On the diaphragm, so he should open it all the way
column17: On the ocular lens, so he should clean it with lens tissue
column28: If the speck were on the slide, it would move when the slide moves, so it is not on the slide. It turns when the ocular lens is twisted, so it is on the ocular lens; clean it only with lens tissue or a soft cloth. Dirt on the objective or the diaphragm would not turn with the ocular.
column29: Use each clue to rule out places. What would the speck do if it were on the slide?

column9: A microscope has a 15x ocular lens. The specimen appears 150 times larger. Which objective is in use? (Type the number only.)
column28: Total = ocular × objective, so objective = 150 ÷ 15 = 10x.
column29: What times 15 equals 150?

column9: Danny's microscope has a 10x ocular, and he is viewing a slide at 1,000x total magnification. He writes: "10 × 1,000 = 10,000, so the objective is 10,000x." What is his mistake?
column14: He should have added; the objective is 1,010x.
column15: He should have subtracted; the objective is 990x.
column16: He multiplied instead of dividing; the objective is 100x.
column17: He made no mistake; the objective is 10,000x.
column28: Total = ocular × objective, so to find a missing objective you divide: 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100x. Check: 10 × 100 = 1,000. ✓ Danny multiplied the total by the ocular, which gives a number far too big. Adding or subtracting lens powers never gives magnification.
column29: Check Danny's answer: would a 10x ocular times his objective really give 1,000x?

column9: Four students each describe one thing they did with the microscope. Which student followed the rules?
column14: Ben: wiped the lenses with a paper towel so they would be extra clean
column15: Ava: watched from the side as she switched to the high-power objective
column16: Cara: used the coarse knob on high power so she could focus faster
column17: Dev: switched to high power first, then centered the specimen there
column28: Ava did it right: watching from the side as the high-power objective swings in lets her make sure it does not hit the slide. Ben should clean lenses only with lens tissue or a soft cloth, because paper towels can scratch them. Cara should never use the coarse knob on high power, and Dev should center the specimen BEFORE switching, because it may disappear from the smaller high-power field.
column29: Check each student against the microscope rules for care, focusing, and switching to high power.

column9: A magnifying glass and a compound light microscope both make things look bigger. Why can the compound microscope magnify so much more?
column14: Its objective lens is much bigger than a magnifying glass lens.
column15: Its ocular and objective lenses both magnify, so their powers add.
column16: It gives a 3D view, so the specimen seems much closer to your eye.
column17: Its ocular and objective lenses both magnify, so their powers multiply.
column28: A magnifying glass is a simple microscope with one lens. A compound microscope uses two or more lenses: the objective magnifies the specimen, then the ocular magnifies that image again, so total magnification = ocular × objective (10 × 40 = 400x). The powers multiply, not add: adding would give only 10 + 40 = 50x. Objective lenses are actually small, so lens size is not the reason, and a 3D view is what a stereoscopic microscope gives, not extra magnification.
column29: Count the lenses in each one. What happens when a second lens magnifies an image that is already magnified?

column9: Microscope A has a 10x ocular and a 40x objective. Microscope B has a 15x ocular and a 20x objective. What is the difference between their total magnifications (larger minus smaller)? (Type the number only.)
column29: Find each microscope's total magnification first, then subtract.
